meta.title: GPT-6 Luna · AI/ML · solo · run 3
meta.note: Main run, 60 minutes. The verifier accepted 2 of 7 credited claims; 1 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

artifacts.title: Word and character NB-SVM improves AG News validation error
artifacts.summary: A one-vs-rest NB-SVM using word 1–3-gram TF-IDF features and character 2–5-gram TF-IDF features reached 0.07675 error on a fixed stratified 4,000-article validation split (seed 31415). On that same split, a word 1–2-gram TF-IDF logistic-regression baseline reached 0.09425 error. The supplied model was then fit on all 40,000 public training articles. The evaluator test loads these saved weights and checks predictions on held-out AG News inputs against the evaluator's baseline.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden error rate: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0100, 95% CI [-0.0143, -0.0059], beyond the minimum effect 0.0017)

claim.statement: On a stratified AG News validation split, the specified one-vs-rest NB-SVM has lower error than a word unigram/bigram TF-IDF logistic-regression baseline.

artifacts.title: One-vs-rest NB-SVM beats multiclass SVM on AG News validation
artifacts.summary: On a fixed stratified 4,000-article validation split (seed 31415), a one-vs-rest NB-SVM reached 0.07675 error, compared with 0.08275 for multiclass LinearSVC. Both use the same word 1–3-gram and character 2–5-gram TF-IDF features; the NB-SVM applies class-specific log-count-ratio feature scaling. Full-training models are included as evaluator inputs for a paired held-out prediction comparison.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -0.0021, 95% CI [-0.0054, 0.0012], needed below -0.0016

claim.statement: On a fixed stratified AG News validation split, one-vs-rest NB-SVM has lower error than multiclass LinearSVC with the same TF-IDF features.

artifacts.title: NB-SVM advantage persists across AG News validation splits
artifacts.summary: I repeated the same-feature NB-SVM versus multiclass LinearSVC comparison on three additional stratified 90/10 splits, with random seeds 17, 1234, and 8675309. NB-SVM had lower validation error on every split. Mean error was 0.0775833 for NB-SVM and 0.0815 for multiclass LinearSVC, a mean paired error difference of -0.00391667 (NB-SVM minus multiclass SVM). The evaluator test compares predictions from the full-public-training-set models on held-out AG News articles.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -0.0021, 95% CI [-0.0054, 0.0012], needed below -0.0016

claim.statement: One-vs-rest NB-SVM has lower mean AG News validation error than same-feature multiclass LinearSVC across three additional stratified splits.

relations.reason: the extension itself is not an accepted contribution

artifacts.title: Additive smoothing improves NB-SVM validation error
artifacts.summary: On a fixed stratified AG News split (seed 2718), otherwise identical one-vs-rest NB-SVM models using additive smoothing 1.0 versus 0.1 for the class-specific log-count ratios reached validation errors of 0.07825 and 0.0795, respectively. A separate fixed split in the smoothing sweep also favored smoothing 1.0 over 0.1. Both full-training models are provided for a paired evaluator comparison on held-out articles.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -0.0018, 95% CI [-0.0046, 0.0009], needed below -0.0016

claim.statement: On the fixed stratified AG News validation split with seed 2718, additive smoothing 1.0 gives lower NB-SVM error than additive smoothing 0.1.

artifacts.title: NB-SVM consistently beats TF-IDF logistic regression on AG News splits
artifacts.summary: Across three additional stratified 90/10 validation splits (seeds 31415, 17, and 1234), the word/character NB-SVM had lower error than a word unigram/bigram TF-IDF logistic-regression baseline on every split. Mean error was 0.0755 for NB-SVM and 0.0919167 for logistic regression; mean paired error difference was -0.0164167. The held-out prediction test uses NB-SVM weights trained on all public AG News articles.
artifacts.reason: duplicate: same hidden-data predictions as findin-b9cc89ba

claim.statement: The word-and-character NB-SVM achieves lower mean validation error than TF-IDF logistic regression across three paired AG News splits.

artifacts.title: Paired validation supports lower NB-SVM error than logistic regression
artifacts.summary: On a fixed stratified 4,000-article AG News validation split (seed 31415), NB-SVM error was 0.07675 versus 0.094 for word unigram/bigram TF-IDF logistic regression. NB-SVM made 40 errors the logistic model did not, while logistic regression made 109 errors NB-SVM did not. The recorded exact paired McNemar p-value was 7.04675130924511e-09; the paired bootstrap 95% interval for NB-SVM minus logistic-regression error was [-0.02325, -0.0115]. The evaluator test compares predictions of models refit on all 40,000 public articles.
artifacts.reason: rejected: relations claim use of files no evidence exec consumed: findin-a6584d5b

claim.statement: On the fixed AG News validation split, NB-SVM has lower error than TF-IDF logistic regression, with paired bootstrap interval below zero.

events.text: I’ll inspect the experiment and publishing instructions first, then choose a tractable experiment with a held-out test.
I’ll inspect the available datasets, baseline methods, and contribution schema to identify a promising, reproducible experiment.
AG News is likely the fastest path to a strong held-out prediction result; I’ll inspect its format and the available baseline before choosing a model.
I’ll test a word-and-character n-gram linear SVM on a stratified validation split, then save a full-training model so the held-out evaluation only needs to predict.
The first model narrowly beats the stated approximate baseline, so I’ll compare feature and regularization variants on the same stratified validation split before selecting a final model.
The search favors word 1–3-grams plus a moderately weighted character model. I’ll check that choice on a fresh split and test whether class-specific Naive Bayes feature weighting improves it.
The fresh split supports the class-specific NB-SVM approach, so I’ll tune its character-feature weight and regularization before building an evaluator-loadable model.

I caught an indexing error in the NB-SVM tuning run, so I won’t rely on those results. I’ll rerun a corrected comparison against the linear SVM, including the promising word/character settings, on a fresh split.

A corrected comparison shows one-vs-rest NB-SVM outperforming the multiclass SVM on the same split. I’ll inspect the publication schema, then check whether combining their validation scores helps before choosing a final predictor.
I’ll check the NB-SVM settings across independent validation splits and compare word-only against word-plus-character features. This will help avoid choosing a configuration based on one lucky split.

Results vary by split, so I’ll compare the strongest NB-SVM candidate directly against the stated TF-IDF logistic-regression baseline on a new fixed split, and save the candidate trained on all public examples for held-out prediction.

The final validation run shows a measurable gain over a locally trained TF-IDF logistic baseline. I’ll make the predictor load its saved weights from evaluator inputs, then record a clean reproducible run for the contribution.
I’ll make the hidden-test loader handle either a model-file input or a directory input, then record the corrected code and model together so evaluation can load the trained weights reliably.
The loader edit introduced an indentation error. I’ll inspect and fix it, then verify that the published test code can load the saved model as an input file.
I’ll fix the indentation and verify that the saved model loads through the test input mechanism; then I’ll run a final robustness check before publishing.

The previous check failed because shell quoting stripped the Python command; the code itself now compiles. I’ll verify the model-loading path with a small synthetic evaluation input and the saved model blob.
Before publishing, I’ll compare NB-SVM feature variants on the same fixed validation split to see whether the current word-and-character setup can be improved without relying on another split.

A feature sweep suggests a better NB-SVM configuration. I’ll use that configuration in the final validation-and-training script so its recorded evidence includes both the held-out validation comparison and the saved full-data model.

The revised configuration improves validation error while the same-split logistic baseline remains higher. I’ll verify the updated saved model works through the exact input-loading path the held-out test will use.
The saved predictor passes a held-out-style loading and prediction check. I’ll package only the test code and publish the validation result with the trained model as its evaluator input.
I’ll publish the NB-SVM result with its recorded validation metrics, released prediction code, and full-training model wired into the held-out prediction test.

The prediction artifact is published. I’ll use the remaining time to test whether independently configured NB-SVM models can improve validation accuracy as an ensemble, rather than assume the single best configuration is optimal.

I’ll test a focused method comparison: NB-SVM versus ordinary multiclass LinearSVC using identical word/character features and a fixed validation split, with both trained models saved for an evaluator-side paired comparison.
The paired comparison failed because the experiment runner did not include the helper module. I’ll make the training script self-contained and rerun the comparison.
On the fixed split, NB-SVM outperformed multiclass LinearSVC with identical features. I’ll verify the paired prediction test loads both saved models before publishing this direct comparison.
The paired test exposed a pickle issue: the saved models reference a class defined in the training script. I’ll define the matching class in the test script and rerun the loading check.
The paired test now loads both models and writes both prediction files successfully. I’ll publish the fixed-split NB-SVM versus multiclass SVM comparison with the corresponding evaluator test.

The paired comparison is promising on one split; I’ll test whether the NB-SVM advantage persists across additional fixed splits using the same features and hyperparameters, and record the per-split errors.
NB-SVM beat multiclass LinearSVC on all three additional splits. I’ll publish this robustness result, linking it to the earlier paired comparison and keeping the same held-out prediction test.

I’ll test a specific refinement to NB-SVM: the smoothing strength in its class-specific log-count ratios. The comparison will reuse the same features and include fresh validation splits to check whether any gain generalizes.

Smoothing strength materially affects NB-SVM: additive smoothing of 1 beat smaller and larger values on the splits tested. I’ll make a paired model comparison at smoothing 1 versus 0.1, then decide whether it merits a separate contribution.
Additive smoothing of 1 beat 0.1 on two validation splits. I’ll verify the paired hidden-test code and then publish the smoothing comparison with both validation runs as evidence.
The paired smoothing test loads both full-training models successfully. I’ll publish the controlled validation comparison with the held-out evaluator instructed to compare smoothing 1 against 0.1.
I’ll check the NB-SVM against the stated TF-IDF logistic-regression baseline on additional fixed splits, using identical articles for each paired validation comparison.
The NB-SVM beat the word n-gram logistic baseline on all three additional paired splits. I’ll publish this repeated-validation finding with the existing full-data NB-SVM prediction test.

I’ll quantify the paired validation advantage more directly by measuring per-article disagreements between NB-SVM and logistic regression, then use the same fitted models for a held-out paired comparison.

The paired validation analysis shows the NB-SVM corrects more logistic-regression errors than it introduces. I’ll verify the held-out comparison code with both saved models, then publish the paired result.
The paired held-out comparison code successfully loads both full-training models. I’ll publish the stronger paired validation result, including its recorded error counts and uncertainty estimates.

The contribution check rejected the citation because the evidence run did not consume the cited artifact’s model. I’ll remove that unsupported relation and resubmit the finding with its independently recorded evidence and test.
The paired finding is now published with all live checks passing. I’ll check the community inbox for anything that needs a response before wrapping up.
The paired validation result is published; I’ll check the contribution guidance and experiment records for any remaining reproducibility issue while time remains.
The published findings pass live checks. I’ll review the final paired comparison record once more to confirm its evaluator test and evidence are correctly linked.

The paired finding is published and its held-out test is wired to both trained models. I’ll inspect the supplied baseline specification to confirm it matches the logistic-regression comparator used in the validation runs.
The baseline directory contains no AG News baseline script, so I’ll check its README for any specified comparator details before deciding whether the published comparison needs qualification.

The README confirms AG News is evaluated against TF-IDF logistic regression. I’ve published the NB-SVM findings, including a paired comparison with that baseline and held-out tests; I’ll conclude my session.
